specPoints.text: know that a covalent bond is formed between atoms by the sharing of a pair of electrons
understand covalent bonds in terms of electrostatic attractions

primer.text: From Ionic Bonding you already know that atoms can reach full outer shells by losing or gaining electrons. Non-metal atoms cannot hand electrons to one another, so this note shows the other route: sharing pairs of electrons, and the electrical attraction that makes each shared pair a strong bond.

lessons.title: Formation of covalent bonds
lessons.opening: Non-metal atoms can reach a full outer shell without forming ions: they share pairs of electrons instead. Each shared pair is one covalent bond, and covalent bonds are very strong. Two chlorine atoms, for example, each supply one electron to a shared pair, and the shared electrons are then counted towards the outer shell of both atoms.
keyPoints: Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons to gain full outer shells.
Each shared pair of electrons is one covalent bond, and the bonds are very strong.
Shared electrons are called bonding electrons and always occur in pairs.
Outer electrons that take no part in the bond are called non-bonding electrons.
Covalently bonded substances are either simple molecular structures, like water, or giant covalent structures, like diamond.

low.restatement: Two non-metal atoms each put one electron into a shared pair, and the pair counts in both outer shells at once. That shared pair is the covalent bond, the bonds are strong, and any outer electrons left unshared are simply non-bonding.
low.analogy: Two neighbours each contribute one brick to build a shared garden wall: the wall belongs to both properties at the same time, and neither owner could claim it alone.
low.examPointer: Say shared, not transferred: writing that electrons are donated or gained in covalent bonding costs the mark that distinguishes it from ionic bonding.

medium.restatement: A covalent bond is a shared electron pair contributed jointly by two non-metal atoms, with the pair occupying the outer shells of both atoms simultaneously. The bond is strong, the shared electrons are the bonding electrons, and the unshared outer electrons remain the non-bonding electrons of their own atoms.
medium.analogy: Picture two authors co-writing one paragraph that appears in both of their books: the same text serves both works, and neither book is complete on its own.
medium.examPointer: Classify substances by structure when asked: simple molecular examples include oxygen and water, while diamond and graphite are the giant covalent examples.

check.stem: What exactly is a covalent bond?

options.text: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
options.explanation: One pair, shared by both atoms, is the whole of the covalent bond.

options.text: A transferred electron from a metal to a non-metal
options.explanation: Transfer between metal and non-metal is ionic bonding; covalent bonding shares instead.

options.text: Any attraction between two non-metal atoms
options.explanation: The bond is specifically the shared pair; other attractions between molecules are far weaker forces.
options.misconception: intermolecular attraction mistaken for the bond

options.text: A pair of protons shared between two nuclei
options.explanation: Protons stay in the nucleus; the shared particles in a covalent bond are electrons.

check.stem: Two chlorine atoms bond covalently. How many electrons does each atom contribute to the shared pair?

options.text: One each
options.explanation: In a normal covalent bond each atom provides one of the two electrons in the shared pair.

options.text: One atom provides both
options.explanation: Both-atoms-from-one descriptions fit dative bonding, which is beyond this course; the normal bond takes one from each.

options.text: Seven each
options.explanation: Seven is each chlorine atom's outer electron count; only one electron from each enters the shared pair.

options.text: Two each, making four shared electrons
options.explanation: Four shared electrons would be a double bond; the single bond between two chlorines shares one pair only.

check.stem: What are the electrons on the outer shell that do not take part in bonding called?

options.text: Non-bonding electrons
options.explanation: Outer electrons untouched by the shared pairs keep their own name: non-bonding electrons.

options.text: Delocalised electrons
options.explanation: Delocalised describes electrons free to move through a whole structure, as in metals; these stay with their own atom.

options.text: Free electrons
options.explanation: The non-bonding electrons remain attached to their atom; they are not free to roam.

options.text: Inner-shell electrons
options.explanation: The electrons in question sit on the outer shell; inner shells are not part of the discussion.

check.stem: Why are covalent bonds described as strong?

options.text: Because a large amount of energy is needed to break the attraction holding the shared pair in place
options.explanation: The shared pair is gripped by both nuclei at once, so breaking the bond costs substantial energy.

options.text: Because the shared electrons move at very high speed
options.explanation: Speed of the electrons is not the measure of bond strength; the energy needed to break the bond is.

options.text: Because the atoms involved are always large
options.explanation: Bond strength does not follow atom size; it follows the strength of the shared-pair attraction.

options.text: Because each bond contains two full outer shells
options.explanation: The outer shells belong to the atoms separately; the bond is the shared pair between them.

check.stem: Which pair of substances correctly illustrates the two structure types that covalent bonding can produce?

options.text: Oxygen, a simple molecular structure, and diamond, a giant covalent structure
options.explanation: Oxygen exists as small separate molecules, while diamond extends covalent bonding throughout a giant lattice.

options.text: Sodium chloride and oxygen, both simple molecular
options.explanation: Sodium chloride is ionic, not covalent, and so is not part of this classification.

options.text: Diamond and graphite, both simple molecular
options.explanation: Both are giant covalent structures; neither exists as separate small molecules.

options.text: Water and sodium, both giant covalent
options.explanation: Water is simple molecular, and sodium is a metal with metallic bonding.

lessons.title: Electrostatic attractions in covalent bonds
lessons.opening: A covalent bond holds because of electrical attraction: the shared pair of electrons is negatively charged, and both atomic nuclei are positively charged, so each nucleus pulls on the same pair. The bond is drawn as a short straight line between the two atoms, and the sharing lets each atom sit in a noble-gas-like arrangement that is more stable.
keyPoints: The shared pair of electrons and both nuclei pull on each other with strong electrostatic attraction.
The electrons in the pair carry a negative charge, and each nucleus carries a positive one, so attraction follows.
A covalent bond is drawn as a short straight line between the two atoms, such as H-H.
The shared electrons are best regarded as charge clouds in constant motion, not as points fixed in place.
Sharing lets each atom reach an arrangement similar to a noble gas, which makes each atom more stable.

low.restatement: Both nuclei pull positively on the same negatively charged shared pair, and that double pull is the glue of the bond. Draw the bond as a line between the atoms, and remember the shared electrons move constantly rather than sitting still.
low.analogy: Two friends each holding one handle of the same shopping bag: the bag stays between them because both are gripping it, just as both nuclei grip the shared pair.
low.examPointer: When asked to explain the bond in terms of attraction, name both parties: the shared pair and the nuclei; omitting the nuclei loses the electrostatic link.

medium.restatement: The bond's strength comes from electrostatics: the negatively charged shared pair sits between two positively charged nuclei, and each nucleus attracts the pair. The electrons form moving charge clouds rather than fixed positions, and the shared arrangement gives each atom a noble-gas-like outer-shell pattern with greater stability.
medium.analogy: Picture a tug-of-war rope gripped by both teams at once: the rope is held taut precisely because two sides pull on the same object, which is the shared pair here.
medium.examPointer: Use the phrase electrostatic attraction between the shared pair and the nuclei; answers that stop at sharing without the attraction rarely reach the explanation mark.

check.stem: Between which two things does the electrostatic attraction of a covalent bond act?

options.text: Between the shared electron pair and the nuclei of both atoms
options.explanation: The negative pair sits between positive nuclei, and each nucleus attracts it, which holds the bond.

options.text: Between the two nuclei directly
options.explanation: Two positive nuclei would repel each other; the shared negative pair between them is what joins the atoms.

options.text: Between the outer shells of the two atoms
options.explanation: Shells are regions, not charges; the attraction acts between the shared pair and the nuclei.

options.text: Between the non-bonding electrons of each atom
options.explanation: Non-bonding electrons repel each other; the bond's attraction centres on the shared pair.
options.misconception: lone-pair repulsion mistaken for the bond

check.stem: How is a single covalent bond represented in a displayed formula?

options.text: A short straight line between the two atoms, as in H-H
options.explanation: One line stands for one shared electron pair, which is one covalent bond.

options.text: A pair of circles overlapping between the atoms
options.explanation: Overlapping circles belong to shell diagrams; the displayed formula uses a line for the bond.

options.text: An arrow from one atom to the other
options.explanation: Arrows suggest transfer, which is the ionic picture; covalent bonds share rather than move electrons.

options.text: The formula letters simply written side by side, as in HH
options.explanation: Side-by-side letters give the formula but show no bond; the line is what marks the shared pair.

check.stem: Why are the shared electrons described as charge clouds rather than fixed points?

options.text: Because the electrons are in a state of constant motion rather than sitting at fixed positions
options.explanation: The shared pair occupies a moving region of space, so a cloud describes it better than a dot.

options.text: Because the electrons are electrically neutral
options.explanation: Electrons carry negative charge; the cloud describes their motion, not a lack of charge.

options.text: Because the cloud belongs to only one nucleus
options.explanation: The shared pair is attracted by both nuclei at once; that is what makes it a bond.

options.text: Because the electrons leave the bond at intervals
options.explanation: The shared pair remains the bond; only its position within the region is in motion.

check.stem: How does sharing electrons make each atom more stable?

options.text: It gives each atom an outer-shell arrangement similar to a noble gas
options.explanation: The shared pair counts towards both outer shells, completing them in the noble-gas manner.

options.text: It gives each atom a full inner shell
options.explanation: Inner shells were already complete; the stability gain sits in the outer shell.

options.text: It turns each atom into a positive ion
options.explanation: No ions form in covalent bonding; the atoms stay neutral while sharing.

options.text: It removes the atom's non-bonding electrons
options.explanation: Non-bonding electrons remain on their own atoms; sharing touches only the bonding pair.

check.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts covalent bonds with ionic bonds?

options.text: Covalent bonds share electron pairs and form no ions, while ionic bonds follow from electron transfer
options.explanation: Sharing without transfer and without ions is the covalent signature; transfer producing ions is the ionic signature.

options.text: Covalent bonds transfer electrons while ionic bonds share them
options.explanation: The two models have been swapped; covalent is the sharing case.

options.text: Both bond types require a metal atom to be present
options.explanation: Covalent bonding happens between non-metals only; the metal requirement belongs to ionic bonding.

options.text: Covalent bonds are always weak and ionic bonds always strong
options.explanation: Covalent bonds are very strong; the weak forces in molecular substances lie between the molecules, not inside them.
options.misconception: bond strength confused with intermolecular strength

glossary.definition: A bond formed between two atoms that share a pair of electrons.
The shared electrons that make up a covalent bond; they occur in pairs.
Outer-shell electrons that take no part in any covalent bond and stay with their own atom.
The positively charged centre of an atom, which attracts the shared electron pair.
The moving region of space in which shared electrons are best described as sitting, rather than a fixed point.

workedExample.prompt: Two chlorine atoms form a molecule of Cl2. a) Describe how the covalent bond forms, stating what each atom contributes. b) Explain why the bond is strong in terms of electrostatic attraction. c) State how the bond is shown in a displayed formula.
steps: a) Each chlorine atom contributes one electron to a shared pair; the pair counts towards the outer shell of both atoms, so each reaches a full outer shell without forming ions.

b) The shared pair of electrons is negatively charged and the two nuclei are positively charged, so strong electrostatic attraction acts between the shared pair and each nucleus and holds the atoms together.
c) A single covalent bond is drawn as a short straight line between the two atoms: Cl-Cl.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Each atom shares one electron — one shared pair forms the bond. b) Electrostatic attraction between the shared pair and both nuclei. c) A short straight line: Cl-Cl.
